slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open by returning to the parallel postulate from Chapter 2. Euclid's fifth postulate says that through a point not on a line, there is exactly one parallel. What happens if there are infinitely many parallels? The result is hyperbolic geometry, a consistent geometry with constant negative curvature. Orient students to printed pages 174 through 212.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the five themes: the upper half-plane and disk models, Mobius transformations as the isometry group, hyperbolic geodesics as semicircles and diameters, the hyperbolic distance metric, and conformal properties that make angles correct even though distances are distorted.

slides.label: Upper Half-Plane
slides.narration: Present the upper half-plane model. The points are the upper half of the complex plane, and the metric is the Euclidean metric scaled by one over the imaginary part. This scaling makes distances near the real axis enormous and distances high up small.

slides.label: Poincare Disk
slides.narration: Present the Poincare disk model as the conformal map of the upper half-plane to the unit disk. Geodesics become circular arcs perpendicular to the boundary circle and diameters. The boundary circle represents infinity.

slides.label: Mobius Transformations
slides.narration: Introduce Mobius transformations as the isometry group of the hyperbolic plane. In the upper half-plane model, these are maps of the form z maps to az plus b over cz plus d with real coefficients and positive determinant.

slides.label: Hyperbolic Distance
slides.narration: Derive the hyperbolic distance formula. In the upper half-plane, the distance between two points is computed by integrating the metric along the geodesic. The formula involves logarithms and captures exponential growth of distances near the boundary.

slides.label: Conformality
slides.narration: Explain conformality: both models preserve angles. A Euclidean angle between two curves at a point equals the hyperbolic angle. Present the three-reflections theorem for hyperbolic isometries paralleling the Euclidean result.

slides.label: Three Curvatures
slides.narration: Connect the three curvature regimes. Spherical geometry has positive curvature and angle excess; Euclidean has zero curvature and angle sum exactly pi; hyperbolic has negative curvature and angle deficit. The parallel postulate determines curvature.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter and the book by showing how the four pillars come together in the study of non-Euclidean geometry. Hyperbolic geometry is the final test case proving the parallel postulate is genuinely independent and consistent geometries with different curvatures are possible.
